description: We are student innovators interested in AI/ML, software development, robotics, mechatronics, astronomy and engineering. We have experience with Python, web development, Arduino, IoT and renewable energy projects, including a working solar energy prototype. We seek enthusiastic teammates skilled in coding, AI/ML, astrophysics, 3D modelling, UI/UX, data science or scientific research. Curiosity, creativity and teamwork matter most. Let's build something extraordinary for space exploration!
summary: OUTPOST ONE: AEGIS is a browser-based 3D mission trainer that places students in command of humanity’s first crewed lunar planetary-defense outpost. Players must keep four specialist astronauts alive by balancing power, oxygen, water, food, radiation shielding, morale, construction, and repairs until resupply arrives. They can directly drive a six-wheel rover to calibrate the AEGIS radar, examine real near-Earth-object close-approach records from NASA’s NeoWs API, and plan an orbital-observatory retarget using a genuine Hohmann transfer and the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation. Dynamic hazards, including dust storms, solar-particle events, micrometeorites, and crew conflict, turn scientific facts into meaningful choices rather than textbook exercises. The project addresses the challenge by making authentic engineering trade-offs clear, interactive, and enjoyable for young learners. It is important because it builds systems thinking, scientific literacy, and confidence with NASA open data while running instantly in any modern browser without installation.
details:
What it does and how it works.
OUTPOST ONE: AEGIS is a realtime 3D mission trainer that runs entirely in a browser. You take
command of AEGIS-1, a four-person lunar planetary-defence listening post in 2046, and you have one
job: keep four astronauts alive until resupply while bringing the outpost's radar online.

Each mission is a run of sols — 24, 28 or 34 depending on tier (Luna Cadet at Sea of Tranquility,
Luna Explorer on the Shackleton rim, Mars Commander on Elysium Planitia), with supply margins,
consumption rates, ambient dose and event pace tuned per tier. You spend build points on eight base
systems — solar array field, battery bank, habitat dome, greenhouse dome, ice extractor rig, radar
and comms mast, med bay and more — and every system has a power draw and a production effect on
four tracked resources: power, oxygen, water and food. Four named crew with distinct roles
(commander, flight engineer, botanist, science officer) gate what the outpost can actually do,
and their health and morale are tracked resources of their own.

Every sol the simulation resolves generation against draw, consumption, radiation dose accumulation
and an event deck: dust storms that slash solar output and demand a panel sweep, solar particle
events where you divert power and shelter the crew in the core, meteorite impacts, brownouts and
crew conflict. You can also send the rover out on an expedition — costing 8 power and adding field
dose — to collect three calibration samples, which feeds radar calibration and science return.

Once the radar is up, the planetary-defence feed populates with real close-approach objects
retrieved from NASA's NeoWs: name, diameter estimate, relative velocity, miss distance and PHA
classification, shown strictly as observation targets. The Orbital Mechanics Lab next to it plans a
two-impulse Hohmann transfer from a 100 km to a 500 km circular orbit: you choose propellant
(monopropellant at 220 s Isp against Lox/methane at 360 s) and propellant mass, and the game solves
the rocket equation live — required Δv, transfer time and the resulting mass ratio.

Benefits. It makes systems thinking physical: cutting radar power to keep the greenhouse alive is
a decision with a face. It builds genuine data literacy, because the target list on screen is a live
NASA API response and a PHA flag is explicitly framed as a classification, not a forecast. It teaches
engineering trade-offs rather than trivia — the rocket equation, closed-loop life support rates and
radiation dose as a budget. And it removes every classroom barrier: one static URL, no install, no
account, no GPU requirement, sessions that fit a lesson period. If the network or API key fails, the
Mission Library falls back to a bundled offline snapshot and says so.

Intended impact. Convert "space facts" into the instinct to manage a system. Give teachers a
drop-in hook for physics (Δv, mass ratios, energy), life science (closed-loop ECLSS, plant growth),
Earth and space science (near-Earth objects, radiation) and computer science. And show that planetary
defence is an operational discipline built on measurement, warning and life support — not movie peril.

Tools, languages, hardware. React with React Three Fiber and Three.js for the realtime 3D scene;
JavaScript/JSX; Vite, which compiles the whole game into a single self-contained web file; Tailwind
CSS for the HUD; the NASA NeoWs REST API through api.nasa.gov; Google Fonts (Orbitron, Space Grotesk,
IBM Plex Mono — SIL Open Font License); Cloudflare Pages for hosting. No special hardware: the target
device is an ordinary laptop or Chromebook. Key art was produced with AI image tools and code was
written with AI assistance, disclosed on the title screen and in the repository notes.

How it is creative. The data is the mechanic, not the decoration — the objects players reason about
are fetched live. A 24-sol clock turns engineering into narrative pressure. The Mission Library prints
a real citation next to every mechanic, so the game teaches its own provenance. The whole thing wears
a "deep-space command deck" identity — near-black, cyan, amber and violet, cinematic lunar art — so it
reads as a game first and a worksheet never. Failure is informative: brownouts and morale collapse are
endings that explain the system that failed.

Factors we considered. Scientific validity versus playability (simplified but never wrong, with
assumptions disclosed); not alarming students (observation targets, PHA explained, no impact
prediction); classroom reality (install-free, low-end hardware, lesson-length sessions, keyboard-first
controls, high-contrast readable HUD); NASA media guidelines (no logos, insignia or flags, no implied
endorsement); AI-use disclosure policy; and scope discipline — six slides, inside the seven-slide limit.
